'''Frank Albert Cotton''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (April 9, 1930 – February 20, 2007)<ref name="royalsoc">{{Cite journal | last1 = Chisholm | first1 = M. H. | last2 = Lord Lewis Of Newnham | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2008.0003 | title = Frank Albert Cotton. 9 April 1930 -- 20 February 2007 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | volume = 54 | pages = 95–115 | year = 2008 | doi-access = free }}</ref> was an American chemist. He was the W.T. Doherty-Welch Foundation Chair and Distinguished Professor of Chemistry at [[Texas A&M University]].  He authored over 1600 scientific articles.<ref name="telegraph"/> Cotton was recognized for his research on the chemistry of the [[transition metal]]s.

==Early life and education==
Cotton, known as "Al" Cotton, or "F Albert" on publications, was born on April 9, 1930, in [[Philadelphia]], [[Pennsylvania]].  He attended local public schools before attending [[Drexel University]] and then [[Temple University]], both in Philadelphia.<ref name="telegraph"/>  After earning his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree from Temple in 1951, Cotton pursued a Ph.D. thesis under the guidance of [[Sir Geoffrey Wilkinson]]<ref name="royalsoc"/> at [[Harvard University]] where he worked on [[metallocene]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Wilkinson | first1 = G. | last2 = Pauson | first2 = P. L. | last3 = Cotton | first3 = F. A. | journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume = 76 | issue = 7 | pages = 1970–1974 | year = 1954 | doi = 10.1021/ja01636a080 | title =  Bis-cyclopentadienyl Compounds of Nickel and Cobalt| bibcode = 1954JAChS..76.1970W }}</ref> He received his [[Ph.D.]] in 1955.<ref name=CurrSci/>

==Career==
Following his graduation from [[Harvard University]], Cotton began teaching at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT). In 1961, at 31-years-old, he became the youngest person to have received a full professorship at MIT.<ref name="telegraph"/>  His work emphasized both electronic structure and chemical synthesis.  He pioneered the study of multiple bonding between transition metal atoms, starting with research on [[rhenium]] halides,<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bertrand | first1 = J. A. | last2 = Cotton | first2 = F. A. | last3 = Dollase | first3 = W. A. | journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume = 85 | issue = 9 | pages = 1349–1350 | year = 1963 | doi = 10.1021/ja00892a029 | title =The Metal-Metal Bonded, Polynuclear Complex Anion in CsReCl<sub>4</sub>  | bibcode = 1963JAChS..85.1349B }}</ref> and in 1964 identified the [[quadruple bond]] in the [[Potassium octachlorodirhenate|{{chem|Re|2|Cl|8|2-}}]] ion.  His work soon focused on other metal-metal bonded species,<ref>Cotton, F. A.; Walton, R. A. "Multiple Bonds Between Metal Atoms" Oxford (Oxford): 1993. {{ISBN|0-19-855649-7}}.</ref> elucidating the structure of chromium(II) acetate.

He was an early proponent of single crystal [[X-ray diffraction]] as a tool for elucidating the extensive chemistry of metal complexes.  Through his studies on clusters, he demonstrated that many exhibited "[[fluxional molecule|fluxionality]]", whereby ligands interchange coordination sites on spectroscopically observable time-scales.  He coined the term "[[hapticity]]" and the nomenclature that derives from it.

In 1962 he undertook the crystal structure of the Staphylococcal nuclease enzyme,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Cotton FA, ((Hazen EE Jr)), Richardson DC |title=Crystalline extracellular nuclease of Staphylococcal nuclease |year=1966 |journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=241 |pages=4389–4390|doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)99732-2 |doi-access=free }}</ref> solved to 2Å resolution in 1969, published in 1971,<ref name="Arnone Bier Cotton Day 1971 pp. 2302–2316">{{cite journal | last1=Arnone | first1=A. | last2=Bier | first2=C.J. | last3=Cotton | first3=F.A. | last4=Day | first4=V.W. | last5=Hazen | first5=E.E. | last6=Richardson | first6=D.C. | last7=Richardson | first7=J.S. | last8=Yonath | first8=A. | title=A High Resolution Structure of an Inhibitor Complex of the Extracellular Nuclease of Staphylococcus aureus | journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=246 | issue=7 | year=1971 | issn=0021-9258 | doi=10.1016/s0021-9258(19)77221-4 | pages=2302–2316| doi-access=free }}</ref> and deposited in the [[Protein Data Bank]] (PDB code 1SNS) as one of the first dozen protein crystal structures.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Richardson JS, Richardson DC |title=Studying and Polishing the PDB's Macromolecules |journal=Biopolymers |doi=10.1002/bip.22108 |pmid=23023928 |pmc=3535681 |volume=99 |issue=3 |date=Mar 2013 |pages=170–82}}</ref>

In 1972 Cotton moved to Texas A&M University as the Robert A. Welch Professor of Chemistry.  The following year he was named the Doherty-Welch Distinguished Professor of Chemistry.  He also served as the director of the university's Laboratory for Molecular Structure and Bonding.<ref name="telegraph"/><ref name="texasam">{{cite news| title =Internationally Prominent Chemist Dr. F. Albert Cotton Passed Away Tuesday At Age 76| publisher =Texas A&M University| date =2007-02-21| url =http://tamunews.tamu.edu/2007/02/21/internationally-prominent-chemist-dr-f-albert-cotton-passed-away-tuesday-at-age-76/| access-date =2011-01-26| url-status =dead| archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20100717064119/http://tamunews.tamu.edu/2007/02/21/internationally-prominent-chemist-dr-f-albert-cotton-passed-away-tuesday-at-age-76/| archive-date =2010-07-17}}</ref>

==Pedagogical influence==
In addition to his research, Cotton taught [[inorganic chemistry]]. He authored ''Chemical Applications of Group Theory''.<ref>Cotton, F. A., ''Chemical Applications of Group Theory'', John Wiley & Sons: New York, (1st ed. 1963, 3d ed. 1990). {{ISBN|0-471-51094-7}}</ref>  This text focuses on [[Group theory|group theoretical]] analysis of [[chemical bond|bonding]] and [[spectroscopy]].

Among college students, Cotton is perhaps best known as the coauthor of the textbook ''Advanced Inorganic Chemistry,'' now in its sixth English edition.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0471199575.html |title=Wiley: Advanced Inorganic Chemistry, 6th Edition |access-date=2012-10-11 |archive-date=2017-07-26 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170726121245/http://www.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0471199575.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=Advanced/>  Coauthored with his thesis advisor, Sir [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]], and now with coauthors Carlos Murillo and Manfred Bochmann, the textbook is colloquially known as "Cotton and Wilkinson."  The text surveys coordination chemistry, cluster chemistry, homogeneous catalysis, and organometallic chemistry.<ref name="telegraph">{{cite news   | title =Professor F Albert Cotton   | publisher = The Daily Telegraph  | date = 2007-03-02  | url =https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1544265/Professor-F-Albert-Cotton.html  | access-date = 2018-04-27}}</ref><ref name=Advanced>Cotton, F. A. and Wilkinson, G., ''Advanced Inorganic Chemistry'', John Wiley and Sons: New York, (1st ed. 1962, 6th ed. 1999). {{ISBN|978-0-471-19957-1}}</ref>

Cotton served on various editorial boards of scientific journals, including those of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'', ''[[Inorganic Chemistry (journal)|Inorganic Chemistry]]'', and ''[[Organometallics]]''. He chaired the Division of Inorganic Chemistry of the ACS and was an ACS Councillor for five years.  He served on the U.S. National Science Board (1986–1998), which oversees the National Science Foundation, and the Scientific and Technical Advisory Committee of Argonne National Laboratory, and the National Research Laboratory Commission of Texas.

Cotton supervised the thesis research of 116 doctoral students<ref name="texasam"/> as well as more than 150 postdoctoral associates,<ref name=CurrSci>[http://www.ias.ac.in/currsci/mar252007/844.pdf Obituary in Current Science '''92''', 844 (25 March 2007)]</ref> including [[Richard H. Holm]], [[Stephen J. Lippard]], [[Charles B. Harris]], [[Tobin J. Marks]], [[John J. Wise]], [[Susumu Kitagawa]] and [[Ada Yonath]]. This academic lineage has become one of the most influential in the field of chemistry, extending to third-generation scholars such as [[Omar M. Yaghi]], [[Jeffrey R. Long]], [[Jeremy M. Berg]], [[Jacqueline Barton]], [[Chuan He]], [[Amy Rosenzweig]], [[Wesley I. Sundquist]], [[John F. Hartwig]], [[JoAnne Stubbe]], [[Paul Alivisatos]], [[Michael D. Fayer]], [[Lawrence Que Jr.]], [[Christopher J. Chang]], [[Ahmed Zewail]], and [[Mercouri Kanatzidis]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Academic Tree |url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/tree.php?pid=52384&fontsize=1&pnodecount=4&cnodecount=2 }}</ref>

==Recognition==
Among the awards Cotton received included the U.S. [[National Medal of Science]] in 1982,<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.cfm?recip_id=90 National Science Foundation – The President's National Medal of Science]</ref> the [[Wolf Prize]] in 2000; and the [[Priestley Medal]], the [[American Chemical Society]]'s highest recognition, in 1998.<ref name="texasam"/>

In 1995, the Department of Chemistry at Texas A&M along with the local section of the American Chemical Society, inaugurated the annual F.A. Cotton Medal for excellence in chemical research.{{cn|date=October 2025}}

A second award named in his honor, the F. Albert Cotton Award for Synthetic Inorganic Chemistry, is presented at the National Meeting of the American Chemical Society each year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/funding/awards/cotton-award-in-synthetic-inorganic-chemistry.html|title=F. Albert Cotton Award in Synthetic Inorganic Chemistry |publisher = American Chemical Society}}</ref>

Cotton was a member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in the [[United States]], and the corresponding academies in [[Russia]], [[China]], the [[United Kingdom]], [[France]], and [[Denmark]], as well as the American Philosophical Society.  He received twenty-nine honorary doctorates.<ref name="texasam"/>

==Run for ACS presidency==
Cotton caused a controversy in his run for President of the American Chemical Society for 1984, wherein he mailed a letter to selected members describing his opponent as "a mediocre industrial chemist".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hargittai |first1=Istvan |title=Candid Science: Conversations With Famous Chemists |date=26 January 2000 |publisher=[[World Scientific]] |isbn=978-1-78326-214-4 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=K_u3CgAAQBAJ |pages=241–242 |access-date=10 April 2022 |language=en}}</ref> Cotton ultimately lost the bid to his opponent Dr. [[Warren D. Niederhauser]] of [[Rohm & Haas]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Niederhauser Serves as ACS President-elect |url=https://digital.library.wisc.edu/1711.dl/FKUSETKZ4Q5WZ87 |access-date=10 April 2022 |work=Badger Chemist Newsletter |issue=30 |publisher=UW-Madison Libraries |date=30 November 1983}}</ref>

==F.A. Cotton Medal for Excellence in Chemical Research==

The F.A. Cotton Medal, established in 1994, is awarded annually by the Texas A&M Section of the [[American Chemical Society]] to recognize accomplishments in research rather than distinction of any other sort, no matter how meritorious. The award is sponsored by the F. Albert Cotton Endowment Fund, which was initially raised by Carlos A. Murillo in honor of Frank Albert Cotton, to whom the first medal was awarded in 1995. The recipient receives, in addition to the medal, a bronze replica thereof and a certificate describing the award.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chem.tamu.edu/medals+lectureships/cotton-medal/|title=F. A. Cotton Medal for Excellence Chemical Research|publisher= Texas A&M Section of the American Chemical Society|access-date= 2 February 2017}}</ref>

==Death==
Cotton died on February 20, 2007, in [[College Station, Texas]] from complications of a head injury he suffered in a fall in October 2006.<ref name="chron">{{cite news   | title = Texas A&M chemist F. Albert Cotton dies at age 76  | publisher = Houston Chronicle  | date = 2007-02-20  | url =https://www.chron.com/news/houston-deaths/article/Texas-A-M-chemist-F-Albert-Cotton-dies-at-age-76-1626629.php  | access-date = 2007-03-14}}</ref>  He was survived by his wife, the former Diane Dornacher, whom he married in 1959, and their two daughters, Jennifer and Jane.<ref name="telegraph"/>
The Brazos County Sheriff's Department opened an investigation into his death, describing his death as "suspicious".<ref name="The Eagle">{{cite news   | title = Professor Cotton's death investigated  | publisher = The Eagle  | date = 2007-04-18  |url =http://www.theeagle.com/news/a_m/professor-cotton-s-death-investigated/article_6ae94cde-757c-5674-a24b-bc7319a73281.html  | access-date = 2018-03-06}}</ref>
